title: Claude Code: when you want to move a lot faster
promise: You'll know how to decide whether Claude Code is for you now or not yet. If it is, you'll have it installed with git in place and a save point made before it touches a single file of yours. And you'll have practiced with your own hands how to go back.
why: Diego is building the website for his climbing gym in Zaragoza with Claude in the chat box. He's already at fourteen files, and every small change means six copy-pastes. One afternoon he pasted the wrong file over the good one. It wiped out the booking form that had cost him two nights of work. Claude Code would have made that same change in forty seconds without him touching a single file. But it could also have rewritten all fourteen at once. That's where almost everyone crashes: they install the fast tool before they install the undo button.

theory.title: The same brain, different hands
theory.text: In the app, Claude only sees what you paste to it and only gives you back text that you have to paste yourself. That back-and-forth is the bottleneck. The AI doesn't think slowly: you're the one acting as messenger between it and your files. Claude Code is that same Claude placed inside a folder on your computer. It opens the files itself, reads them all, edits them, and runs things. Here's a question that's bound to come up: is it also smarter? The answer is no. It's exactly the same model, with the same tendency to make things up and the same quirks. What changes is the hands, not the head. That has a consequence, and it's worth understanding before you install anything. In the chat, a bad answer costs you a copy-paste. Here, a bad answer has already touched nine files while you were looking at another tab. You gain speed, not accuracy. Speed multiplies whatever you were already doing, good or bad.
theory.analogy: In the chat it's like explaining a leak to a plumber over the phone. You go to the bathroom, tighten what he tells you, come back, and report what happened. Claude Code is the plumber inside your house, toolbox open. It's the same plumber. But now, if he makes a mistake, he makes it directly on your pipes.
theory.example: Diego wanted to change the contact phone number on his site, which appeared in fourteen files. By hand, searching and pasting from the chat: twenty-two minutes, and he missed one. With Claude Code: forty seconds, and all fourteen done.

theory.title: The sign that it's your turn, and the sign that it isn't yet
theory.text: Almost nobody makes this jump at the right moment. It's usually made too early. And then, instead of building, you spend two weekends fighting an installation. The signs that it is your turn are concrete and you'll recognize them at a glance. Your project passes five or six files. You copy-paste more than ten times per session. You already have something working, even if it's ugly. And you're afraid to touch anything because you don't know what will break. The signs that it isn't your turn yet are just as concrete. You're still deciding what to build. Everything you have fits in one file. Or you've never seen your project running in the browser. If you're in the second group, the chat box will serve you better and more cheaply. It's not a failing grade: the tool is built for a different moment. The rule that works is this: make the jump when copy-pasting is what eats the most of your time. Don't make it because a video told you Claude Code is the future. There's also a silent requirement almost nobody mentions. To review what it does, you need to have seen your project work at least once. If not, you have nothing to compare against.
theory.example: Diego, with fourteen files and fifteen copy-pastes an afternoon: it's his turn. Marta has spent three days on a single 200-line index.html. She's never opened it in a browser. It's not her turn yet, and skipping this now saves her a whole weekend.

theory.title: What it's going to demand of you: a terminal, money, and attention
theory.text: First is the terminal: the dark window where you type commands with the keyboard instead of clicking buttons. It's worth measuring how much respect you give it correctly. You'll use it for three things your whole life: opening it, entering your folder, and typing the word claude. From there you type in English, same as in the chat, in that same window. Second is money. Claude Code comes with Claude Pro, about $20 a month. That plan has a usage cap that recharges every five hours, and if you work hard you'll hit it. The next tier up is about $100 a month. The free plan doesn't include it. Another option is using an API key instead of a subscription (pay per use, like a taxi meter). With that, a long afternoon can run you $15 to $30 without you noticing. Set a spending limit on your account before you start. And third, which is the real cost: attention. It will ask your permission before every change, and saying yes without reading is exactly the same as having no permissions set at all. If you're going to do something else while it works, better not open it today.
theory.example: A normal two-hour session with Claude Pro: twenty or thirty requests, zero extra dollars because it's included in the plan. The same session with an API key and no cap set: between $8 and $20, and you find out when the charge arrives.

theory.title: Why git isn't just advisable — it's mandatory
theory.text: Claude Code writes directly to your hard drive. There's no unsaved tab, no "Save As." There's no moment between it deciding and it doing. And the three kinds of undo you think cover you don't cover you. Ctrl+Z only works inside the file you have open, and it dies when you close it. The recycle bin doesn't catch what's been overwritten, because nothing was ever actually deleted there. And automatic backups from OneDrive or iCloud can take hours to notice. Git solves that. It's a free program that takes snapshots of your whole folder at a given moment. It lets you go back to any of them with a button. Each snapshot is called a commit, and you make one when something works. With that in place, your worst day goes from "I lost two nights of work" to "I lost twenty minutes." That difference is the whole lesson. There's also a side effect nobody tells you about that's worth more than the safety net: with git in place, you dare. You let it try big things, whole reorganizations, weird ideas, because going back costs one click. Without git you work with your teeth clenched and ask for small, timid things. That's the exact opposite of what the tool is for. And one detail that says it all. On Windows, Anthropic requires git to be installed for Claude Code to work. They didn't put that there for decoration.
theory.analogy: It's the saved game in a video game. Without saving, every boss fight is played to the death and you end up avoiding the hard parts. With the save file, you go for it, because losing costs three minutes.
theory.example: Diego made a commit, asked for "reorganize the navigation across the whole site," it touched eleven files and came out worse than before. "Discard all changes" button, four seconds, everything back to how it was. Without git, that same mistake is two afternoons.

theory.title: How to talk to it so it doesn't wreck anything
theory.text: Three habits and that's it, and all three are learned in one session. The first is plan mode. You ask it to investigate and tell you what it's going to do before touching anything. You read it, correct it if needed, and only then approve. The second is the size of the request. "Fix the website" is a bad request in the chat too, but here it's expensive. In the chat it only gives you back text; here it rewrites files. "in booking.html, add a phone field to the form and don't touch anything else" is a good request. The third is one request, one commit: you save after every change that works. If you chain five requests and then something breaks, you have no way of knowing which one broke it. And you end up throwing away all five. Beyond the habits there's the permissions screen, which is your brake. Before every edit it shows you the lines it's going to remove in red and the ones it's going to add in green. Then it asks if it should proceed. Read them even if you don't understand the code: what you're checking is the size. If you asked for a phone field and see four hundred lines changed, something got away from it. The "yes, and don't ask me again" option is convenient for editing files and dangerous for running commands. And the mode that skips permissions entirely carries the word dangerously in its own name. It's there on purpose.
theory.example: Bad request: "make the website more modern." Good request: "in index.html and contact.html, change the body font to a cleaner sans-serif. Don't touch colors, don't touch the menu, don't install anything. When you're done, tell me which files you touched."

theory.title: What going faster doesn't fix
theory.text: Claude Code doesn't decide what to build or whether it's worth building, and it moves just as fast toward a good idea as toward a bad one. It also doesn't see your website: it works with the text of the files, not with what shows on screen. That's why it can leave you a button that's flawless in the code and hideous to look at. For it to weigh in on appearance, you have to take a screenshot and paste it in. And there's a slow trap that catches a lot of people. Since asking for things costs so little, in three weeks you have sixty files you can't explain. From there it starts failing more too. The project has become a mess, and a mess is harder for anyone to read. The people who really go fast with this aren't the ones asking for more things per hour. It's the ones who pause every so often, open what's there, check with their own eyes that it works, and save it before continuing. Going fast doesn't save you from understanding what you have; it saves you from writing it.
theory.analogy: It's a much faster car, not a GPS. You're still the one choosing the destination, and taking the wrong exit at 200 gets you further away, faster, than taking it at 40.

tasks.title: Decide whether it's your turn or not yet
tasks.where: In the Claude or ChatGPT app, in a new chat
tasks.action: Before installing absolutely anything. Open a new chat and paste the message below, filling in the blanks with the truth, not with what you'd like it to be. To count the files, open your project folder in the file explorer and count them by eye. If the answer you get is "not yet," you've just saved yourself an entire weekend of installations.
tasks.prompt:
I want to decide whether it makes sense for me to jump to Claude Code or whether I'm still better off pasting code into the chat box. I'm not a programmer and I have no experience with the terminal.

MY SITUATION:
- What I'm building: [DESCRIBE IT IN ONE SENTENCE]
- How many files it has right now: [NUMBER]
- Does any of it work already, even if it's ugly? [YES / NO / PARTIALLY]
- Have I ever seen it open in a browser? [YES / NO]
- How many times I copy-paste between the chat and my files in a typical session: [APPROXIMATE NUMBER]
- Have I ever lost work by pasting something over the good version? [YES / NO]
- Operating system: [WINDOWS / MAC]

WHAT I WANT FROM YOU:
1. A verdict in the first line: "it's your turn" or "not yet." Only one of the two.
2. The two specific reasons from MY situation you're basing it on. From my data, not from theory.
3. If the verdict is "not yet": what exactly has to happen for it to become "yes." Give me something checkable, like a file count or a concrete milestone, not "when you feel ready."
4. If the verdict is "it's your turn": what I'll need to install and how much it'll cost me per month in dollars.

RULES: don't sell me the tool. If my case is one that's better off in the chat, tell me plainly, no sugarcoating. No intro, no closing summary.
tasks.expect: A verdict in the first line, no beating around the bush. With fewer than five files and nothing working yet, "not yet" is normal, and that's a good result. With twelve files and fifteen copy-pastes a session it'll tell you yes, and you'll know what the next nine tasks are for.
tasks.stuck: If it says yes to everything without looking at your data, it's sided with you. Push back with: "Answer me with only one of these two sentences and nothing else: it's your turn / not yet." And if the verdict is "not yet," really stop here. Come back in two weeks with a bigger project: the rest of the lesson will still be waiting for you.

tasks.title: Install git and the window that manages it
tasks.where: In your browser, then on your computer
tasks.action: Two downloads, both free, fifteen minutes. First git, which is the engine: go to git-scm.com and click the big download button for your system. Open the downloaded file and click "Next" on every screen without changing anything. There are about eight, and the defaults are the right ones. If you have a Mac you can skip this part. Open the Terminal app and type git --version. If you don't have it, macOS will offer to install it in a popup: accept and wait a few minutes. Second, GitHub Desktop. It's the window with buttons that saves you from ever typing git commands. Go to desktop.github.com and click "Download for Windows (64bit)" or the Mac button. It installs and opens on its own. On the welcome screen it asks you to sign in. You don't need an account for any of this. Look for the small link at the bottom that says "skip this step" and click it. Then it asks for a name and email to sign your save points: put in your own and click "Finish."
tasks.expect: GitHub Desktop open, with a screen that says "Let's get started!" and three big boxes. To check git installed correctly: on Windows press Start, type cmd, open it, type git --version and press Enter. You should see something like "git version 2.47.1." On Mac, the same from Terminal.
tasks.stuck: If git --version says it doesn't recognize the command, it's almost always the same thing. Close that black window completely with the X and open a new one. Freshly installed programs only exist for windows you open afterward. If it still doesn't show up, run the git-scm.com installer again and this time don't change any checkboxes.

tasks.title: Turn your folder into a project with history
tasks.action: Menu "File" at the top left, then "Add local repository..." inside it. Click "Choose..." and find the folder where your project is. Since that folder doesn't have history yet, a warning will show in red. It says "This directory does not appear to be a Git repository." Right below it there's a blue link that says "create a repository." Click it. A window opens with the name already filled in. In the "Git ignore" dropdown, choose "Node" if your project is a website with installed dependencies. Leave it on "None" if you just have loose text files. Click the "Create repository" button. Now on the left you'll see the list of all your files, each with its checkbox checked. At the very bottom there's a small box that says "Summary (required)." Type starting point there and click the blue "Commit to main" button.
tasks.expect: The list on the left goes empty and the center shows "No local changes." If you click the "History" tab at the top you'll see a single line: "starting point," with your name and the time. That's your first snapshot, and you can always go back to it, whatever happens next.
tasks.stuck: If the list on the left has thousands of files and you see a folder called node_modules, don't commit yet. Those are the dependencies: they take up a huge amount of space and shouldn't be saved. Create a file called .gitignore inside your folder with Notepad. Write the line node_modules inside it and save. You'll see the list drop to a few dozen. If you already committed with the thousands of files, it's not serious: it works the same, just slower.

tasks.title: Rehearse undoing before you need it
tasks.where: In your folder and in GitHub Desktop
tasks.action: This is the fire drill and it's the most important task in the lesson. Doing it now is what will let you work without fear half an hour from now. Open any file in your project with Notepad (TextEdit on Mac). Delete half the screen of content, brutally, and save with Ctrl+S. Go back to GitHub Desktop: that file already shows in the list on the left. In the center you see everything you removed, in red. Now right-click on the file's name in the list and choose "Discard changes..." A confirmation popup appears: click "Discard Changes." Open the file again and look at it.
tasks.expect: The file is exactly as it was, with everything you deleted back in place, and the list on the left empty again. That button, and the "Commit to main" button, are literally all you need to know about git for everything that comes next.
tasks.stuck: If "Discard changes" shows up grayed out, it's because you didn't save the file after deleting: save it and check again. A warning about what actually is permanent: discarding throws away everything done SINCE the last snapshot. If there's something you want to keep, commit before discarding. As a safety net, GitHub Desktop sends what's discarded to the system trash. Worst case, you can still rescue it from there.

tasks.title: Install Claude Code and open it for the first time
tasks.action: On Windows: press Start, type PowerShell, and open "Windows PowerShell." On Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, and open it. This is the window that feels intimidating. You're going to type three things into it your whole life, and this is the first. Copy and paste this exact line and press Enter. On Windows: irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex . On Mac: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash . It's Anthropic's official installer and should only come from claude.ai or the official docs. If you find it copied on a forum or in a video, don't run it. When it finishes, close the window entirely and open a new one — this part matters. Type claude --version and press Enter. Then type claude by itself. The first time it asks about the text color and asks you to log in. Choose "Log in with your Claude account": your browser will open and you just need to authorize.
tasks.expect: After claude --version you should see a version number. After claude, the window changes appearance. The name "Claude Code" appears, a box to type in at the bottom, and a line showing the folder it's working in. From here on you don't type commands: you type in English, same as in the chat.
tasks.stuck: If claude --version says it doesn't recognize the command, it's almost certainly that you didn't close and reopen the window. Close it with the X and open another. If logging in tells you your plan doesn't include Claude Code, you need Claude Pro (about $20/month) or above. The free plan doesn't include it. If on Windows it complains it can't find git, task 2 didn't get finished. Go back to git-scm.com, install it, and open a new terminal.

tasks.title: Ask it to map your project without touching anything
tasks.where: Inside Claude Code, in your project folder
tasks.action: First you need to get it into your folder, and there's a trick so you don't type the path by hand. In the terminal type cd followed by a space. Then drag your project folder from the file explorer onto the black window. The path types itself. Press Enter. Now type claude and press Enter. When the input box appears, paste the message below. Notice that the first order you give it is to read, not to touch. You want to see how it moves before handing it a hammer.
tasks.prompt:
Before anything else, a rule for this message and the next one: don't modify, don't create, and don't delete any file. Read only.

Read through this whole folder and explain to me what's in it, talking to me like someone who has never coded before. I want:

1. What this project is for, in two sentences, based on what you actually see in the code and not on what you imagine from the folder name.
2. A list of the files that actually matter, one line each: what it does and in what situation I'd touch it. Config files and files I'll never open, group them all into a single line at the end.
3. Which file you'd open first if you wanted to change how the home page looks.
4. Three things you see that are wrong or half-finished, ordered from most to least painful, and why each one hurts.
5. One thing about the project you don't understand and need me to clarify.

No general theory about websites. Talk only about what's in this specific folder. Translate any technical word in parentheses the first time you use it.
tasks.expect: You'll see it opening files on its own, one after another, without asking permission (reading doesn't need it, only writing). At the end, a summary where you recognize your project: your file names, your text, your sections. If it describes something that isn't yours, you're in the wrong folder.
tasks.stuck: If it says the folder is empty, cd didn't work. Type /exit to leave and look at the first line of the window: that shows the path you're in. If it's not your project's, repeat the drag-the-folder trick. On Windows, if the path has spaces or accents, put it in quotes: cd "C:\Users\Diego\My Site".

tasks.title: Make your first real request, in plan mode
tasks.action: Before typing anything, press Shift+Tab twice. At the bottom, in the status bar, you'll see the mode change and something like "plan mode on" appear. In that mode it investigates and proposes a plan to you. But it doesn't touch a single file until you approve. Now ask for ONE small, specific change. One. Use the template below and change only the first line. When it presents the plan, read it in full before approving. If something doesn't add up, don't approve: tell it what's wrong and have it redo it.
tasks.prompt:
CHANGE I WANT: [ONE THING ONLY, AND SPECIFIC. For example: "on the contact page, add a phone field to the form and make it required"]

FILES YOU CAN TOUCH: whatever's needed for that and nothing else.
FILES YOU CANNOT TOUCH: [IF THERE'S ANY YOU'RE AFRAID TO BREAK, NAME IT HERE].

BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING, tell me:
1. Which files you're going to modify and what you'll change in each, one line per file.
2. What could break in what's already working.
3. How I check with my own eyes, in the browser, that it came out right. Step by step.

RULES:
- Don't take the opportunity to fix other things you notice along the way. If you see something, list it at the end and I'll decide.
- Don't install anything new without asking me first and explaining what it's for.
- If the change is going to touch more than three files, stop and tell me: I'd rather split it into two requests.
- I'm not a programmer. Translate any technical word in parentheses the first time you use it in each session.
tasks.expect: A plan written out on screen and, at the end, a question with options to approve or reject it. When you approve, it starts asking permission file by file. It shows you in red the lines it's removing and in green the ones it's adding, and asks if it should proceed. That red and green is what's about to happen on your hard drive in a second, so look at it even if you don't understand it.
tasks.stuck: If Shift+Tab doesn't do anything visible, forget the shortcut. You get the plan the same way with the three questions in the message, which are there for exactly that. If it proposes touching nine files for a one-line change, don't approve. Reply "too much. Just make me the phone field and don't touch anything else" and it'll come back with a much shorter plan.

tasks.title: Review what it did and save it
tasks.where: In GitHub Desktop, then in your browser
tasks.action: Switch to GitHub Desktop without closing Claude Code. In the list on the left are all the files it touched. In the center you see, line by line, what it removed in red and what it added in green. Look at it even if you don't understand the code: what you're checking is the amount, not the syntax. If you asked for a phone field and see six files touched and four hundred lines changed, something got out of hand. Then open your project in the browser and check with your eyes two things. That the change is there, and that everything next to it still works. Only then go back to GitHub Desktop, type something like phone field on contact page in the "Summary" box, and click "Commit to main."
tasks.expect: The list on the left empty again and a new line in the "History" tab. From that moment that state of your project is safe no matter what happens next. A good commit message is one that, three weeks from now, tells you which point to go back to without opening anything.
tasks.stuck: If you look at it in the browser and something's broken, don't fix it by hand and don't ask for another change on top of the broken one. Right-click the list on the left, "Discard all changes...", and ask for it again with a smaller, more explicit request. Undoing and repeating costs two minutes; fixing on top of something broken costs the whole afternoon and almost never works.

tasks.title: Leave your rules in writing in CLAUDE.md
tasks.action: Claude Code reads a file called CLAUDE.md in your folder on startup, and treats what's inside as permanent instructions. It's the difference between repeating "don't touch the design" fifteen times and saying it once. Type /init and press Enter: it reads the project and creates that file for you on its own, with the basics. Then paste the message below, filling in the blank, to add your own rules.
tasks.prompt:
Add a section at the end of the CLAUDE.md file titled "How to work with me" with these rules, as written, only adapting the file names to what actually exists in this project:

- I'm not a programmer. Explain any technical word in parentheses the first time you use it each session.
- One request, one change. Don't take the chance to fix things I didn't ask for along the way: list them at the end and I'll decide.
- Before touching more than three files, stop and ask me.
- Don't install new dependencies without telling me first what they are, what they're for, and whether it can be done without them.
- Don't delete files. If you think one is unnecessary, tell me and I'll delete it.
- Never touch [PUT THE FILE YOU'RE MOST AFRAID OF BREAKING HERE] without warning me first.
- When you finish something that works, remind me to make a save point before moving on to the next thing.

When you've written it, show me the whole file so I can read it.
tasks.expect: A CLAUDE.md file in your folder with your rules inside. In GitHub Desktop it'll show up as a new file, so give it its commit. You'll notice it in the next session: it'll stop proposing changes you didn't ask for and will warn you before diving into something big.
tasks.stuck: If /init tells you CLAUDE.md already exists, even better: you already had it and you just need to add the rules. If the rules don't seem to take effect, it's almost always because the session was already open before you wrote them. Type /exit, come back in with claude, and now it reads them on startup.

tasks.title: Cause a disaster and undo it in twenty seconds
tasks.where: Inside Claude Code, with the commit from task 8 already made
tasks.action: This is the rehearsal with the tool in place, and it's what will really take away your fear. First check that GitHub Desktop has nothing pending in the list on the left. If it does, commit before continuing. Now ask for something deliberately ambitious, the kind you wouldn't dare ask for at another time. Paste the message below, let it do the whole thing, look at it in the browser. And then undo it, even if you like it: this is a rehearsal, not a real change.
tasks.prompt:
Reorganize the visual look of the whole project: change the font, the color palette, and the spacing to make it look more modern, and apply the change across every page there is.

Do it all in one go, without asking me page by page. When you're done, tell me in a single line how many files you touched and how many lines you changed in total.
tasks.expect: A good pile of touched files. Go to GitHub Desktop and there's the whole mess, counted and laid out. Now right-click the list on the left and choose "Discard all changes..." A popup tells you how many files you're about to discard. Click "Discard Changes." Reload your project in the browser: it's exactly as it was. That, and nothing else, is what lets you work fast without gritting your teeth.
tasks.stuck: If you liked how it turned out and hate to throw it away, throw it away anyway and ask for it again afterward. It'll come out similar in a minute, and the rehearsal is worth far more than the design. If after discarding the browser still shows you the strange version, press Ctrl+F5 (Cmd+Shift+R on Mac). That makes it forget what it had cached.

matters: Git in place with a commit made BEFORE the first order, never after. Claude Code writes straight to your disk: there's no unsaved tab. Ctrl+Z doesn't cross fourteen files, and the trash doesn't catch what's been overwritten. The people who abandon this tool aren't the ones who ask for things badly. It's the ones who lost an afternoon of work on day three and never trusted it again.

Reading the permissions screen instead of clicking "yes" out of habit. That screen is your entire brake, and accepting without looking is having a brake and never pressing it. The "don't ask me again" option is convenient for editing files and risky for running commands. And the mode that skips permissions entirely carries the word "dangerously" in its name. Someone decided that needed a warning.

One request, one commit. If you chain five requests and then something stops working, there's no way to know which one broke it. You end up throwing away all five, including the three that were fine. Saving after every change that works costs ten seconds and turns "everything's broken" into "I'll go back to the point from twenty minutes ago."

What you leave inside the folder. Claude Code reads everything that's in there. What goes into a commit stays in the history forever, even if you delete the file afterward. Passwords, access keys, exports with customer data, or invoices don't belong in the project folder. Getting something out of the history once it's in is a considerable hassle, so it's much cheaper not to put it in at all.
ignore: Subagents, hooks, and MCP. These are ways to split work among helpers, to have something trigger automatically at certain moments, and to connect other tools to it. They're real and useful, but they solve problems that show up once you're already working this way every day. Right now they'd just add pieces you wouldn't know how to turn off the day they fail.

Choosing the perfect tool among Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, Gemini CLI, or Cursor. For what matters here, they're very similar: they read your folder, edit files, ask your permission, and need git exactly the same way. Learn the habit with one and switching to another will cost you an afternoon, not a course.

Real git: branches, merges, remotes, pull requests. It's an entire professional tool and you don't need it for this. Committing and discarding changes covers almost everything that'll happen in your first month. You'll learn the rest the specific day you need it.
canDo: Read a folder of forty files in a minute and tell you in plain English what's in it and what each thing does. It doesn't matter if the code was written by someone else or by it three weeks ago.
Make the same change across fourteen files without skipping any or getting the place wrong. It's exactly what a person in a hurry is worst at and what it's best at.
Run something, read the error that comes up, understand what's failing, and try again on its own, several times in a row. You don't have to copy the error anywhere.
Set up the boring scaffolding: installing what's needed and starting your website on your own computer. And tell you the exact address to type in the browser to see it.
cantDo: See your website. It works with the text of the files, not with what shows on screen. That's why it can leave you a button that's flawless in the code and dreadful to look at. For it to weigh in on appearance you have to take a screenshot and paste it in.
Decide what to build or whether it's worth building. It moves just as fast toward a good idea as toward a bad one. Checking the map every so often is still on you.

Recover what it's overwritten if there are no save points. It has its own undo within the session, but that ends when you close the window. Without git, what's overwritten is gone and there's no one to appeal to.

Log into your accounts, buy a domain, enter your card, or publish something in your name. And if you ever hand it the keys to do one of those things, you're really handing them over. Between its decision and your bank account there's no layer of common sense waiting in between.
words: Terminal

The dark window where you type commands with the keyboard instead of clicking buttons. It has a reputation for being hard, but for this you only use it for three things: opening it, entering your folder, and starting the tool.
Claude Code
The version of Claude that works inside a folder on your computer. It opens your files, changes them, and runs things on its own. It doesn't give you back text for you to paste by hand.
Git
A free program that keeps taking snapshots of how your folder looks at each moment. That way you can go back to any of them when something goes wrong. It's invisible: it works underneath everything.
Commit
Each one of those snapshots. You give it a short name, like "contact form finished," and from then on that state is safe no matter what happens next.
Repository
A folder that already has that snapshot history turned on. It's the same folder as always, with the same files, just that now it remembers where it's been.
Discard changes
The button that returns your folder to the last snapshot you made and throws away everything touched since then. It's the real undo, and it works even if forty files were changed at once.
Diff
The view that shows you, line by line, what was removed (in red) and what was added (in green). It's what you look at before saying yes to a change.
Plan mode
A mode where it first tells you what it plans to do and waits for your approval. It doesn't touch a single file until you give it. It turns on by pressing Shift+Tab twice.
CLAUDE.md
A text file you leave in your folder with your rules written inside. It's read at the start of every session, so you don't have to repeat them every day.
Dependency
A piece of software made by other people that your project needs to work. They download themselves, take up thousands of files, and that's why it's worth telling git to ignore them.
